title: True sonship and those who falsely claimed it
source_text: Ἔτι δὲ πρὸς τὸν σωτῆρα αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰουδαῖός φησιν ὅτι, εἰ τοῦτο λέγεις, ὅτι πᾶς ἄνθρωπος κατὰ θείαν πρόνοιαν γεγονὼς υἱός ἐστι θεοῦ, τί ἂν σὺ ἄλλου διαφέροις; πρὸς ὃν ἐροῦμεν ὅτι πᾶς μὲν ὁ, ὡς ὁ Παῦλος ὠνόμασε, μηκέτι ὑπὸ φόβου παιδαγωγούμενος ἀλλὰ δι᾿ αὑτὸ τὸ καλὸν αἱρούμενος υἱός ἐστι θεοῦ· οὗτος δὲ πολλῷ καὶ μακρῶ διαφέρει παντὸς τοῦ διὰ τὴν ἀρετὴν χρηματίζοντος υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ, ὅστις ὡσπερεὶ πηγή τις καὶ ἀρχὴ τῶν τοιούτων τυγχάνει. ἡ δὲ τοῦ Παύλου λέξις οὕτως ἔχει· „οὐ γὰρ ἐλάβετε πνεῦμα δουλείας πάλιν εἰς φόβον, ἀλλ᾿ ἐλάβετε πνεῦμα υἱοθεσίας, ἐν ᾧ κράζομεν· Ἀββὰ ὁ πατήρ.“ τινὲς δὲ καὶ ἐλέγξουσιν, ὥς φησιν ὁ παρὰ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖος, μυρίοι τὸν Ἰησοῦν φάσκοντες περὶ ἑαυτῶν ταῦτα εἰρῆσθαι, ἅπερ περὶ ἐκείνου ἐπροφητεύετο. οὐκ οἴδαμεν οὖν εἰ ὁ Κέλσος ἠπίστατό τινας ἐπιδημήσαντας τῷ βίῳ καὶ τὸ παραπλήσιον βουληθέντας ποιεῖν τῷ Ἰησοῦ καὶ θεοῦ υἱοὺς αὑτοὺς ἀναγορεύειν ἢ θεοῦ δύναμιν. ἐπεὶ δὲ φιλαλήθως τὰ κατὰ τοὺς τόπους ἐξετάζομεν, ἐροῦμεν ὅτι Θευδᾶς πρὸ τῆς γενέσεως Ἰησοῦ γέγονέ τις παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις „μέγαν“ „τινὰ ἑαυτὸν“ λέγων· οὗ ἀποθανόντος οἱ ἀπατηθέντες ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ διεσκεδάσθησαν. καὶ μετ᾿ ἐκεῖνον „ἐν ταῖς τῆς ἀπογραφῆς ἡμέραις,“ ὅτ᾿ ἔοικε γεγεννῆσθαι ὁ Ἰησοῦς, Ἰούδας τις Γαλιλαῖος πολλοὺς ἑαυτῷ συναπέστησεν ἀπὸ τοῦ λαοῦ τῶν Ἰουδαίων ὡς σοφὸς καὶ καινοτομῶν τινα· οὗ καὶ αὐτοῦ δίκας τίσαντος ἡ διδασκαλία καθῃρέθη πάνυ ἐν ὀλίγοις καὶ ἐλαχίστοις μείνασα. καὶ μετὰ τοὺς Ἰησοῦ δὲ χρόνους ἠθέλησε καὶ ὁ Σαμαρεὺς Δοσίθεος πεῖσαι Σαμαρεῖς ὅτι αὐτὸς εἴη ὁ προφητευόμενος ὑπὸ Μω(??)σέως Χριστὸς, καὶ ἔδοξέ τινων τῇ ἑαυτοῦ διδασκαλίᾳ κεκρατηκέναι. ἀλλὰ τὸ εἰρημένον πάνυ σοφῶς ὑπὸ τοῦ ἐν ταῖς Πράξεσι τῶν ἀποστόλων ἀναγεγραμμένου Γαμαλιὴλ οὐκ ἄλογον παραθέμενον δεῖξαι, πῶς ἐκεῖνοι μὲν ἀλλότριοι τῆς ἐπαγγελίας ησαν, οὔτε υἱοὶ θεοῦ οὔτε δυνάμεις ὄντες αὐτοῦ, ὁ δὲ Χριστὸς ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἀληθῶς ην υἱὸς θεοῦ. εἶπε δ᾿ ἐκεῖ ὁ Γαμαλιήλ· „ὅτι ἐὰν ᾖ ἐξ ἀνθρώπων ἡ βουλὴ αὕτη καὶ ὁ λόγος οὗτος, καταλυθήσεται,“ ὡς καὶ τὰ ἐκείνων κατελύθη ἀποθανόντων· „ἐὰν δὲ ᾖ ἐκ θεοῦ οὐ δυνήσεσθε καταλῦσαι τὴν τούτου διδασκαλίαν, μή ποτε καὶ θεομάχοι εὑρεθῆτε.“ ἠθέλησε δὲ καὶ Σίμων ὁ Σαμαρεὺς μάγος τῇ μαγείᾳ ὑφελέσθαι τινάς. καὶ τότε μὲν ἠπάτησε, νυνὶ δὲ τοὺς πάντας ἐν τῇ οἰκουμένῃ οὐκ ἔστι Σιμωνιανοὺς εὑρεῖν τὸν ἀριθμὸν οἶμαι τριάκοντα, καὶ τάχα πλείονας εἶπον τῶν ὄντων. εἰσὶ δὲ περὶ τὴν Παλαιστίνην σφόδρα ἐλάχιστοι· τῆς δὲ λοιπῆς οἰκουμένης οὐδαμοῦ τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ, καθ᾿ ἣν ἠθέλησε δόξαν περὶ ἑαυτοῦ διασκεδάσαι. παρὰ γὰρ οἷς φέρεται, ἐκ τῶν Πράξεων τῶν ἀποστόλων φέρεται· Χριστινανοὶ δ᾿ εἰσὶν οἱ ταῦτα περὶ αὐτοῦ λέγοντες, καὶ ἡ ἐνάργεια ἐμαρτύρησεν ὅτι οὐδὲν θεῖον ὁ Σίμων ἦν.
pass_a_gloss: Further the Jew in him says to the Saviour (σωτήρ) that, if you say this, that every man (ἄνθρωπος) having come to be according to divine providence (θεία πρόνοια) is son (υἱός) of God, in what would you differ (διαφέρω) from another? To whom we shall say that everyone who, as Paul named, is no longer being tutored (παιδαγωγέω) under fear (φόβος) but chooses (αἱρέομαι) the good (τὸ καλόν) for its own sake is son of God; but this one differs by much and far from everyone styled (χρηματίζω) son of God on account of virtue (ἀρετή), who is as it were a certain spring (πηγή) and source/beginning (ἀρχή) of such. Paul's passage runs thus: you did not receive a spirit (πνεῦμα) of slavery (δουλεία) again into fear but received a spirit of adoption (υἱοθεσία), in which we cry (κράζω) Abba, Father (πατήρ). And some will also refute (ἐλέγχω), as the Jew in Celsus says, myriads (μυρίοι), Jesus, claiming (φάσκω) that the things prophesied about him were said about themselves. We do not know then if Celsus knew some having sojourned (ἐπιδημέω) in life and having wished to do the like (παραπλήσιος) to Jesus and proclaim themselves sons of God or power (δύναμις) of God. But since we examine truth-lovingly (φιλαλήθως) the matters of the passages (τόπος), we shall say that Theudas before the birth (γένεσις) of Jesus arose among Jews saying himself to be someone great; on whose dying those deceived (ἀπατάω) by him were scattered (διασκεδάννυμι). And after him in the days of the census (ἀπογραφή), when Jesus seems to have been born, a certain Judas the Galilean drew many away with himself into revolt (συναφίστημι) from the people of the Jews as wise and innovating (καινοτομέω) something; on whose also paying the penalty (δίκας τίνω) the teaching (διδασκαλία) was destroyed (καθαιρέω), remaining among quite few and fewest. And after the times of Jesus Dositheus the Samaritan also wished to persuade Samaritans that he was the Christ prophesied by Moses, and seemed to have prevailed (κρατέω) over some by his teaching. But it is not unreasonable, setting out what was said very wisely by Gamaliel recorded in the Acts (Πράξεις) of the apostles, to show how those were alien (ἀλλότριος) to the promise (ἐπαγγελία), being neither sons of God nor his powers, but the Christ Jesus was truly son of God. Gamaliel said there: if this counsel (βουλή) and this word (λόγος) is from men it will be dissolved (καταλύω), as also theirs were dissolved when they died; but if it is from God you will not be able to dissolve this one's teaching, lest you be found God-fighters (θεομάχος). Simon the Samaritan magician (μάγος) also wished by magic (μαγεία) to steal away (ὑφαιρέομαι) some. And then he deceived, but now it is not possible to find Simonians (Σιμωνιανοί) all in the inhabited world (οἰκουμένη) in number, I think, thirty, and perhaps I said more than there are. They are around Palestine very fewest; of the rest of the world nowhere his name, through which he wished to scatter glory (δόξα) about himself. For among whom it is carried (φέρεται), it is carried from the Acts of the apostles; Christians are those saying these things about him, and the evidence (ἐνάργεια) has testified (μαρτυρέω) that Simon was nothing divine.
pass_b_english: Again, his Jew says to the Saviour: “If you say this, that every human being who has come into being by divine providence is a son of God, how would you differ from anyone else?” To him we shall reply that everyone who is no longer schooled by fear, but chooses the good for its own sake, is, as Paul named him, a son of God. But the Saviour differs greatly, and by a long way, from everyone who is called a son of God because of virtue, for he is, as it were, a kind of spring and source of all such. Paul’s words run like this: “For you did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you received a spirit of adoption, in which we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15).

“Some, too,” as Celsus’s Jew says, “countless people, will refute Jesus, claiming that what was prophesied of him was said of themselves.” We do not know, then, whether Celsus knew of any who came into the world and wished to do something like what Jesus did, and to proclaim themselves sons of God or a power of God. But since we examine these matters with a love of truth, we shall say that a certain Theudas arose among the Jews before the birth of Jesus, “saying that he was somebody great”; and when he died, those he had deceived were scattered (Acts 5:36). After him, “in the days of the census” (Acts 5:37), about the time when Jesus seems to have been born (Luke 2:1–2), a certain Judas the Galilean led many of the Jewish people to revolt with him, as a wise man and one bringing in something new. When he too paid the penalty, his teaching was overthrown, and it survived only among a very small number indeed.

After the time of Jesus, too, Dositheus the Samaritan wished to persuade the Samaritans that he was the Christ prophesied by Moses, and he seemed to have won some over by his teaching. But it is not unreasonable to quote what was said, very wisely, by Gamaliel, as recorded in the Acts of the Apostles, to show how those men were strangers to the promise, being neither sons of God nor powers of his, while Christ Jesus was truly the Son of God. Gamaliel said there: “If this plan and this word are from men, they will be overthrown,” as the movements of those men were overthrown when they died; “but if it is from God, you will not be able to overthrow this man’s teaching, or you may even be found fighting against God” (Acts 5:38–39).

Simon the Samaritan magician also wished to steal some away by his magic (Acts 8:9–11). At that time he did deceive them; but now, I think, it is not possible to find Simonians in the whole world numbering thirty in all, and perhaps I have put the number higher than it is. There are very few of them around Palestine, and in the rest of the world, through which he wished to spread his glory, his name is nowhere found. For wherever it is known, it is known from the Acts of the Apostles; it is Christians who say these things about him, and the plain facts have borne witness that Simon was nothing divine.

choices.choice: Celsus's Jew is quoted twice in direct speech; both are in double quotation marks with the Greek's attributions ('his Jew says to the Saviour', 'as Celsus's Jew says'). In the second, the Greek interrupts the quotation (τινὲς δὲ καὶ ἐλέγξουσιν, ὥς φησιν..., μυρίοι...), so the attribution stands inside it, and 'Some, too, ... countless people' keeps the Greek's pairing of τινές with μυρίοι; exactly where Celsus's words end is not certain. 'As Paul named him' attaches ὡς ὁ Παῦλος ὠνόμασε to the title 'son of God' (Romans 8:14-15); 'no longer schooled by fear' (παιδαγωγούμενος) may echo Galatians 3:24-25 (possible allusion, not cited inline). 'But the Saviour differs' renders οὗτος δέ; the name is supplied from the opening sentence (where the Jew addresses the Saviour), because a bare 'he' after 'to him we shall reply' would point back to the Jew. Romans 8:15: both 'spirit of slavery' and 'spirit of adoption' are anarthrous in the Greek and kept lower-case; many read the second as the Holy Spirit. 'A power of God' may glance at Acts 8:10 (Simon called 'the power of God that is called Great'); not cited inline. Theudas: Origen quotes 'somebody' (τινὰ ἑαυτόν, Acts 5:36) and 'great' (μέγαν, which Acts 8:9 uses of Simon), blending the two. Origen's own chronology places Theudas before the birth of Jesus, following Gamaliel's order; kept as he states it. 'In the days of the census' is Acts 5:37; the link to Jesus's birth alludes to Luke 2:1-2. Gamaliel's words (Acts 5:38-39) are quoted freely: Origen has ὁ λόγος οὗτος for Acts' τὸ ἔργον τοῦτο and 'this man's teaching' for 'them'; the clause 'as the movements of those men were overthrown when they died' (τὰ ἐκείνων) is Origen's interjection and stands outside the quotation marks. The Greek verb is singular with two subjects (ᾖ ... ἡ βουλὴ αὕτη καὶ ὁ λόγος οὗτος); English needs 'are ... they'. 'The Christ prophesied by Moses' alludes to Deuteronomy 18:15-18 (uncited, since Origen gives no wording). 'Strangers to the promise' may echo Ephesians 2:12 (possible). Staged text: Μω(??)σέως read Μωσέως (Moses); ησαν/ην read ἦσαν/ἦν; Χριστινανοὶ read Χριστιανοί. 'Christ Jesus' renders ὁ Χριστὸς ὁ Ἰησοῦς.
'every human being born by divine providence' to 'who has come into being by divine providence' (γεγονώς, broader than birth)
'But he differs' to 'But the Saviour differs' (οὗτος; bare 'he' after 'To him we shall reply' read as the Jew); noted
'“And some,” as Celsus’s Jew says' to '“Some, too,”' (καί was untranslated; δέ needs no 'And' at the head of a quotation)

Gamaliel: 'this plan and this word is ... it will be overthrown' to 'are ... they will be overthrown' (English agreement); 'the cause of those men' to 'the movements of those men' (τὰ ἐκείνων); 'lest you be found fighting even against God' to 'or you may even be found fighting against God' (archaic 'lest'; καί placed as 'even')
'where it is spoken of at all, it is spoken of from the Acts' to 'wherever it is known, it is known from the Acts' (φέρεται: is current)
